stem: A nurse teaches a client with COPD to use pursed-lip breathing during episodes of breathlessness. Which explanation of the technique is accurate?

options.A: Breathe in slowly through the nose, then exhale slowly through pursed lips for longer than the inhalation; this helps keep airways open longer and reduce trapped air.
options.B: Breathe in through pursed lips and exhale quickly through the nose; shortening exhalation helps move air out before the smaller airways begin to narrow.
options.C: Exhale as forcefully and rapidly as possible through tightly pursed lips; the high expiratory flow is what prevents airway collapse and relieves breathlessness.
options.D: Use short, rapid breaths through pursed lips during both inhalation and exhalation; increasing the breathing rate is the main way the technique reduces air trapping.

rationale: Current NCBI StatPearls guidance defines pursed-lip breathing as a deliberate inhalation through the nose followed by a slow, controlled exhalation through pursed lips that prolongs expiration. The expiratory backpressure creates a small amount of positive pressure that helps resist airway collapse, reduces air trapping, and can reduce dyspnea and work of breathing. Current American Lung Association teaching likewise instructs slow nasal inhalation followed by a longer, slow exhalation through pursed lips and explains that keeping the airways open longer helps remove trapped air. Therefore A is correct. B reverses the technique and shortens expiration, C substitutes forceful rapid exhalation for controlled prolonged exhalation, and D promotes rapid shallow breathing rather than the slower breathing pattern used to relieve breathlessness.
educational_objective: Teach pursed-lip breathing in COPD as slow nasal inhalation followed by a longer, controlled exhalation through pursed lips to help keep airways open longer, reduce trapped air, and relieve dyspnea.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf, StatPearls; American Lung Association
source_version_date: StatPearls article last updated January 25, 2025 and published in the 2026 StatPearls edition; American Lung Association patient resource current in 2026
source_locator: StatPearls Pursed-lip Breathing > Definition/Introduction: deliberate inhalation through the nose followed by slow controlled exhalation through pursed lips prolongs the expiratory phase and generates a small amount of positive expiratory backpressure; this helps prevent airway collapse, supports more complete exhalation, reduces air trapping, and reduces dyspnea/work of breathing. > Clinical Significance: properly performed pursed-lip breathing can reduce work of breathing and alleviate respiratory distress. American Lung Association > Pursed Lip Breathing: inhale slowly through the nose, exhale slowly and gently through pursed lips, make exhalation longer than inhalation; keeping airways open longer helps remove trapped air and relieve shortness of breath.
source_claim_supported: Pursed-lip breathing uses slow nasal inhalation and prolonged controlled exhalation through pursed lips; expiratory backpressure helps keep airways open longer, reduce air trapping, and relieve dyspnea in obstructive lung disease.

supporting_sources.locator: Technique instructions: breathe in slowly through the nose, purse the lips, and breathe out slowly and gently through pursed lips; try to exhale longer than inhaling. Mechanism explanation: the technique keeps airways open longer, helps remove trapped air, slows breathing, and relieves shortness of breath.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: The practical teaching sequence and symptom-relief explanation match the StatPearls physiologic description.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed pp. 46–48 (PDF pp. 50–52): manage the care of a client with impaired ventilation/oxygenation; educate client regarding an acute or chronic condition; apply knowledge of nursing procedures, pathophysiology and psychomotor skills for alterations in body systems; educate client about managing health problems; implement interventions to manage recovery from illness.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — COPD breathing technique for impaired ventilation and dyspnea self-management
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four explanations to remove the uniquely-long keyed response and test the actual breathing mechanics rather than relying on obviously false treatment-substitution wording. The item was remapped to Physiological Adaptation because it concerns COPD ventilation and client self-management of breathlessness.

audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies COPD and episodic breathlessness and asks for mechanism/technique rather than claiming that pursed-lip breathing replaces medical treatment.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects the current StatPearls and American Lung Association technique and mechanism; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — it sounds mechanically plausible but reverses the route and shortens expiration, opposite the source-described prolonged controlled exhalation.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — forceful rapid exhalation may intuitively seem to empty lungs faster, but pursed-lip breathing relies on slow controlled prolonged exhalation and expiratory backpressure rather than maximal flow.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — the technique is used during dyspnea, but it slows and controls the breathing pattern rather than deliberately increasing respiratory rate with rapid shallow breaths.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only alternative that correctly states both execution and intended expiratory effect.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B shortens/reverses expiration, C uses forceful rapid expiration, and D promotes rapid shallow breathing.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all four options are essentially matched in length and technical detail and the keyed answer is not uniquely verbose.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Physiological Adaptation directly includes impaired ventilation/oxygenation management and education for acute or chronic illness.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether faster or more forceful exhalation could also reduce trapped air. Current sources consistently specify slow, controlled, prolonged exhalation through pursed lips and attribute benefit to expiratory backpressure and longer airway patency; A remains uniquely correct.
